title: Benediction and the Tantum Ergo
hookLine: a blessing with the monstrance, and a hymn written by Aquinas

cards: At the end of adoration, something changes in the room. Incense rises. People who've been sitting quietly for an hour stand and start to sing, in Latin, a slow old melody.
The priest puts on a long shawl that covers his hands. He lifts the gold monstrance and turns to face everyone. A bell rings.
And instead of the people coming to the Eucharist, it's as if the Eucharist comes to them.

teach.b: Benediction comes from Latin, bene, well, and dicere, to say: a blessing, a speaking well. It's the name for the short service that usually closes Eucharistic adoration. Here's its shape.

The people sing a hymn, often the Tantum Ergo. The priest incenses the host. After a prayer, he wraps his hands in the humeral veil, that long shawl, so it's clear the blessing comes from the Eucharist, not from him.

teach.h: THE VEIL, THE SIGN OF THE CROSS.
teach.b: He lifts the monstrance and makes the sign of the cross with it over the people, in silence, while a bell rings. Then the host is returned to the tabernacle. The hymn is worth knowing.
Tantum Ergo is the last two verses of a longer hymn, Pange Lingua, written by Thomas Aquinas, the great thirteenth-century theologian, for the new feast of Corpus Christi.
Tradition says the Pope asked him to compose the prayers for that feast. It opens: "Tantum ergo Sacramentum veneremur cernui." Roughly: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship.

teach.h: FAITH SUPPLIES WHAT EYES CAN'T SEE.
teach.b: Then it says, in effect, that faith fills in where the senses fail: what the eyes can't see, faith supplies.

Aquinas wrote enormous books of careful reasoning, and his early biographers report that near the end of his life he stopped writing, saying all he'd written seemed like straw compared to what he had seen.
Here, in a short hymn, the thinker bows. That's the spirit of Benediction: after the watching, you don't reach for the blessing. You stand still, and it comes to you.

how: Benediction usually closes a time of Eucharistic adoration: the people sing the Tantum Ergo, the priest or deacon blesses them with the monstrance in silence while a bell rings, and the host is returned to the tabernacle.

o: a blessing given with the host in the monstrance
the closing hymn sung at the end of every Mass
a short prayer of thanks said before a meal

games.q: you're the priest at Benediction. you're about to lift the monstrance. what do you put on first?
o: a long veil that covers your hands.
nothing: you use your bare hands.
games.why: the humeral veil: it covers his hands so the blessing is clearly from the Eucharist, not from him.

practice: Sit or stand still, hands open on your knees or at your sides, and picture the moment the monstrance is lifted toward you, or simply a warm light turning your way.
You don't earn it, and you don't reach for it; you stay still and let it come. If you pray, you can bow your head.

wordCard.voice: Benediction. From the Latin for speaking well. The blessing with the monstrance that closes adoration, sung in with Aquinas's Tantum Ergo. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. The opening of Aquinas's hymn.
